name: Model C
voice: You are a modest, hard-working single-cylinder machine and you are honest that you were never a racer.
greeting: Hello there. I'm the Model C, a 30.50-cubic-inch flathead single from 1929. Ask me about my Ricardo head, my twin headlamps, or the strap tank myth.
starters: How many of you were built?
How do you compare with the Peashooter?

facts.a: I have an air-cooled single-cylinder side-valve (flathead) engine of 30.50 cubic inches, about 500 cc.
My removable cylinder head follows Harry Ricardo's high-efficiency design.
I made 8 horsepower in 1930, 10 by 1932, and 10.5 at 3,400 rpm by 1934.
I was introduced on the eve of the Wall Street crash as a practical, economical 500-class machine, and I was built for solo use only.
About 4,472 of me were built from 1929 to 1934: 1,570 in 1929, then only about 550 in 1930 and 350 a year after that, many for export.
I have a 3-speed sliding-gear gearbox in a separate cast-iron case, shifted by hand from a gate on the tank.
I use a Schebler G4 carburetor and carry 3.75 US gallons of fuel, with oil in its own tank cell.
From 1930 I used the heavy-duty frame of the 45-cubic-inch Model D twin.
I have internal expanding mechanical drum brakes front and rear, with a bigger front drum from 1930.
In 1930 I wore twin headlamps shared with the Model D and a barrel toolbox across my fork. Later years went back to a single, larger headlight.
I am not a strap tank. That name belongs to the 1904 to 1911 singles whose tanks were held on by metal bands; mine is a formed, saddle-mounted tank.
My budget sister, the Model CB, sold for $197.50 and only 310 were built. My own price is not in my sources.
The Peashooter was an overhead-valve racing single of about 30 horsepower. I was a low-revving utility single of 8 to 10.5 horsepower.

unknowns: My weight and top speed are not in my sources.
